extraction.name: VoiceAssistant-Eval
extraction.description: VoiceAssistant-Eval comprises 10,497 curated examples spanning 13 task categories. These tasks include natural sounds, music, and spoken dialogue for listening; multi-tum dialogue, role-play imitation, and various scenarios for speaking; and highly heterogeneous images for viewing.
extraction.creator: Ke Wang, Houxing Ren, Zimu Lu, Mingjie Zhan, Hongsheng Li
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected by extracting diverse visual and auditory inputs from 37 existing datasets, and synthesizing speech instructions using text-to-speech models to replace original text instructions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: During the data curation process, the authors encountered incomplete or inappropriate items, including cases with missing or broken audio or images, as well as instances with ill-posed questions or incorrect answers. These instances were filtered out and removed.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Source data was collected from 47 datasets in total, including 23 audio understanding datasets, RoleBench for role profiles, 22 other datasets for speaking tasks, and MMMU for viewing tasks.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Text instructions were preprocessed by replacing special tokens with descriptive phrases, rewriting text using Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct for better TTS suitability, and rephrasing multiple-choice options. Speech was then synthesized and evaluated, regenerating any clips scoring below 3.8 on UTMOS.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A four-stage curation process was used: (1) Deduplication using lexical overlap and Levenshtein distance, (2) Validation to exclude incomplete or unsuitable instances (corrupted images, silent audio, ill-posed prompts, incorrect answers), (3) Categorization into 13 tasks, and (4) Balanced sampling.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Curators reviewed each item on a single screen with inline players, viewers, transcripts, and multiple-choice options, assigning a Good or Bad verdict along with optional notes based on media integrity, task well-posedness, and answer validity.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, F5-TTS, ChatTTS, Dia-1.6B, UTMOS Strong, Whisper-Large-v3
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors will maintain a data governance process for auditing and removal, reserving the right to update assets if consent or licensing concerns arise.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset includes role-play voice imitation and speaker similarity evaluation, which involves identifiable speaker voices.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to enable research on personalization while minimizing harms related to impersonation, privacy violations, and unequal performance across demographics.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset may carry biases from its source data and design choices, such as a monolingual focus (mostly English) and a fixed set of 100 roles that may encode stereotypes or omit important user personas.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Limitations include limited linguistic diversity (mostly English), lack of dynamic/continuous interaction tasks (e.g., live audio streams or video narratives), and offline/static evaluation that misses real-time deployment factors like latency and barge-in.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluation of voice assistants. It is not supposed to be used for training models for cheating.

name.evidence: We introduce VoiceAssistant-Eval , a comprehensive benchmark designed to assess AI assistants across listening, speaking, and viewing.

description.evidence: VoiceAssistant-Eval comprises 10,497 curated examples spanning 13 task categories. These tasks include natural sounds, music, and spoken dialogue for listening; multi-tum dialogue, role-play imitation, and various scenarios for speaking; and highly heterogeneous images for viewing.

license.evidence: The VoiceAssistant-Eval data and our open-source code are under an MIT license.

creator.evidence: Ke Wang1,∗ Houxing Ren1,∗ Zimu Lu1 Mingjie Zhan2,† Hongsheng Li1,3,†

inLanguage.evidence: Although we include five Chinese roles in the role-play task, all other prompts and evaluations are in English.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: When collecting test data, we first extract diverse visual and auditory inputs from 37 datasets, including natural sounds, music, dialogue, and various images... To replace the original text instructions, we synthesize speech instructions using three advanced text-to-speech (TTS) models

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: When collecting test data, we first extract diverse visual and auditory inputs from 37 datasets... we synthesize speech instructions using three advanced text-to-speech (TTS) models

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: We collect source data from 23 audio understanding datasets... For role-playing, we use the role profiles and question texts from RoleBench... Other source data are from 22 datasets... we select MMMU as the source dataset.

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: We preprocess the texts to ensure high synthesis quality: 1. Image references: We replace special tokens... 2. Text rewriting: We use Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct to rewrite the text so it is more suitable for TTS... 3. Multiple-Choice Questions: We rephrase the options for better readability. During speech synthesis, we use UTMOS Strong to evaluate the generated speech and regenerate it until the score surpasses 3.8.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: We improve data quality through a four-stage curation process: (1) Deduplication: We use lexical overlap and Levenshtein distance to flag potential duplicate questions... (2) Validation: We exclude incomplete or unsuitable instances, including entries with corrupted images, silent audio, ill-posed prompts, and demonstrably incorrect answers... (3) Categorization... (4) Sampling: We sample data from the categorized problems to balance the ratio of different tasks.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: Curators review each item on a single screen, with inline players and viewers, transcripts, and multiple-choice options when present, and then assign a Good or Bad verdict, along with optional notes.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: To operationalize the validation step described in the main text, we build a lightweight web-based curation tool that standardizes quality checks across modalities.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: We use Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct (Qwen et al., 2025) to rewrite the text... We synthesize speech for question texts using three advanced text-to-speech (TTS) models: F5-TTS, ChatTTS, and Dia-1.6B... we use UTMOS Strong to evaluate the generated speech... Finally, we use Whisper-Large-v3 to transcribe the synthesized audio back into text

rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan.evidence: We will maintain a data governance process for auditing and removal and reserve the right to update assets if consent or licensing concerns arise.

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: because the benchmark includes role-play voice imitation and speaker similarity evaluation, we emphasize strict consent, provenance, and anti-impersonation safeguards.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: These measures aim to enable research on personalization while minimizing harms related to impersonation, privacy violations, and unequal performance across demographics.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Like many benchmarks, VoiceAssistant-Eval may carry biases from its source data and design choices... The role-play subset uses a fixed set of 100 roles and associated style prompts. These roles may encode stereotypes or omit important user personas.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: This monolingual focus may not capture the full variability of real user interactions... there remain gaps in task coverage and scenario realism... VoiceAssistant-Eval evaluates models in an offline, static manner, which might not capture certain practical deployment factors.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We intend for researchers to use this dataset to better evaluate voice assistants and, consequently, facilitate future studies in this area. The VoiceAssistant-Eval dataset is not supposed to be used, though the risk exists, for training models for cheating.
